system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2150-12-04 05:26:00 to 2150-12-05 14:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with recurrent abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting that returned after eating tacos, following a recent hospital discharge. She reported collapsing at home in her vomit, prompting re-evaluation. CT imaging showed no acute abdominal pathology, consistent with prior unremarkable studies. Pain and nausea were managed with IV fluids, Dilaudid, and Zofran, with gradual advancement to oral intake. Her chronic pancreatitis was considered the likely contributor, though no active inflammation was seen. A mild Sjogren’s flare with facial erythema and low-grade fever was noted but remained asymptomatic. She tolerated a soft diet, had no pain, and was discharged home with instructions to resume all home medications and follow up with her PCP and rheumatologist. H. pylori treatment was deferred pending outpatient coordination.

radiology_notes.text:
CT OF THE ABDOMEN AND PELVIS

INDICATION:  Right upper quadrant and epigastric tenderness to palpation. 
History of prior pancreatic resection, and splenectomy.

COMPARISON:  Multiple priors, most recently CT of the abdomen and pelvis from
___.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
only, including multiplanar reformations.

CT ABDOMEN:  Visualized lung bases are clear.  Post-surgical change from prior
distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy is stable.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding, or other evidence of pancreatitis.  Remaining pancreatic
parenchymal is normal in appearance.  Intra-abdominal parenchymal organs and
vasculature are otherwise normal in appearance.  There is no free air, free
fluid, or abnormal intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy.

CT PELVIS:  Pelvic loops of large and small bowel and genitourinary structures
are normal.  There is no free pelvic fluid or abnormally enlarged pelvic or
inguinal lymph node.

Visualized skeletal structures are unchanged.  Congenital nonunion of the
posterior elements at L5 is unchanged.  

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of pancreatitis.  Stable post-surgical appearance
status post distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy.  No acute intra-abdominal
process.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with history of pancreatitis, status post partial
pancreatectomy and total splenectomy, now presenting  with right upper
quadrant pain and negative ___ sign.  Evaluate for biliary disease.

COMPARISON:  ___.

RUQ ULTRASOUND:  The liver is normal in echotexture without focal lesion. The
gallbladder is nondistended, without evidence of gallstones.  There is no
pericholecystic fluid.  The CBD is normal in caliber measuring about 3 mm in
diameter.  There is no evidence of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal
dilatation.  The pancreas is seen truncated, consistent with pancreatectomy.
There is no ascites.  There is normal hepatopetal portal venous flow.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of obstructive biliary disease.  Patent portal vein.
No evidence of acute cholecystitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I started having sharp abdominal pain yesterday around 3 PM. It was in my upper belly and then moved to the right side. I’ve had this before, like with my pancreas issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Did the pain get worse? Did you vomit or have any other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I threw up twice and kept dry-heaving. Couldn’t keep anything down. The pain got worse, and my boyfriend said my heart rate was up to 160. That’s when we came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You were dehydrated when you arrived, so we’ve started IV fluids. We also gave you Dilaudid and Zofran for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is better now. But I’m worried—could this be another pancreatitis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re evaluating that. You’ve had a CT scan and an ultrasound of your abdomen to check for any issues with your pancreas or gallbladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they said no active pancreatitis. I still get these flares though, even after the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of chronic pancreatitis can still cause episodes like this, even after the distal pancreatectomy. We’re checking to make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back. There’s no sign of acute pancreatitis or any other abdominal emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging shows stable changes from your past surgery. No gallstones or bile duct blockage either. We think this is a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, possibly triggered by dehydration or your recent methotrexate dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did get my methotrexate shot yesterday—just increased to 25mg. I always feel nauseous after it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely be a factor. We’ll keep monitoring you and make sure you stay hydrated. We’ll also continue managing your pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lab results are back. Your lipase level is normal, which supports that this isn’t acute pancreatitis. Your liver enzymes were a bit elevated, but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about my blood counts? I’m often anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is a bit low, consistent with your history of malabsorption and iron deficiency. But it’s stable, so no need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I take B12 and iron at home, but I know my body doesn’t absorb well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your malabsorption is something to manage long-term. We’ll make sure you continue your supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I haven’t vomited since last night, and the pain is mild now. Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can start with small sips of water. If that goes well, we’ll advance to clear liquids and then a soft diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m really hungry, but I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down water and apple juice. We’re going to switch your IV fluids down and get you a soft meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back—no infection. That’s good. It rules out a UTI as a cause of your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having some blood in my urine lately—still being checked out, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your primary team is still working up the hematuria. But today’s symptoms don’t seem related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated a soft diet well. No vomiting or pain. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if you continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Should I restart all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, including your methotrexate, Plaquenil, omeprazole, and pancreatic enzymes. We’ll send you home with the same meds you came in on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about the methotrexate making me sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause nausea, so take it after a meal. Your rheumatologist may want to review the dose, especially since it was just increased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s your pain? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain. A little tired, but that’s normal for me. I had a full meal and felt fine after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep monitoring overnight, but you’re on track for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without issues. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe this was a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, likely worsened by dehydration and your methotrexate. No signs of acute disease on imaging or labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be sure to drink more fluids and take my enzymes with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And follow up with your PCP within the week. Call if you have severe pain, vomiting, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge instructions ready soon. You can go home once the nurse reviews everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check. You’re still feeling well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no pain, no nausea. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to take all your medications as prescribed, stay hydrated, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic if needed, but hopefully not!

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with acute abdominal pain and vomiting, consistent with a flare of her chronic pancreatitis, in the setting of recent methotrexate administration and dehydration. She was treated with IV fluids, anti-nausea medication, and pain control, with significant improvement. Imaging, including CT and ultrasound, showed no acute abdominal pathology or biliary disease. Labs revealed no elevation in lipase, supporting absence of acute pancreatitis. She tolerated advancement to a soft diet, remained symptom-free, and was discharged home on her baseline medications with instructions to follow up with her primary care provider. The hospital course was uncomplicated.
